blocks.text: Cardiovascular disorders are the leading cause of death in developed and developing countries. They involve the disorders of the blood vessels and heart, and atherosclerosis and arteriosclerosis are their major contributors.

items: Atherosclerosis means deposition within arteries. Various materials may accumulate in the arteries: fatty materials, abnormal amounts of smooth muscle cells, cholesterol, fibrin and cellular debris of various kinds. All these build-ups impair the proper functioning of the arteries, and the accumulation of cholesterol is thought to be the prime contributor. Atherosclerosis can lead to heart attacks, because it narrows the arteries and increases the risk of thrombus formation.

Arteriosclerosis means hardening of the arterial walls. It occurs when calcium is deposited in the arterial walls; blood flow through these arteries is restricted and they cannot expand normally, which forces the heart to work harder. Severe atherosclerosis usually leads to arteriosclerosis.

blocks.text: Various diagnostic tests are performed on cardiovascular patients to locate the exact problem and measure the severity of the disease; the important ones are the ECG and angiography. Coronary angiography is an X-ray examination of the blood vessels or chambers of the heart. A physician guides a small tube-like device, a catheter, through the large arteries of the body; when its tip reaches the opening of the coronary arteries, a special fluid (a contrast medium or dye) that is visible to the X-ray machine is injected through the catheter, and pictures (angiograms) of the fluid in the coronary artery are obtained. If clots are present in the lumen of a coronary artery, the artery appears narrow. By changing the diagnostic catheter to a guiding catheter, physicians can also pass an instrument into the coronary artery; the most commonly used instruments are guide wires and balloon dilation catheters.

Thrombosis is the formation of a thrombus, a solid mass or plug of blood constituents (a clot) in a blood vessel, which may block the vessel wholly or in part. A thrombus may form because of irritation or infection of the lining of the blood vessels, a reduced rate of blood flow due to long periods of inactivity, or diseases such as pneumonia, tuberculosis and emphysema. Thrombosis blocks the blood flow to organs: a thrombosis in the coronary arteries causes a heart attack, and a thrombus in the vessels of the brain causes a stroke. A thrombus may be dislodged and carried to some other location in the circulatory system; such a thrombus is an embolus, and the formation of a thrombus and its carriage elsewhere is thromboembolism.

The coronary arteries supply oxygen and nutrients to the cardiac muscle. If blood flow in them is blocked, one or more parts of the cardiac muscle receive an insufficient supply, and if heart muscle dies for want of oxygen and nutrients the condition is myocardial infarction, a heart attack. Blockage of the coronary arteries is usually due to the gradual build-up of lipids, especially cholesterol, in the inner wall of a coronary artery. If such conditions persist, chest pain called angina pectoris can result during periods of stress or physical exertion; angina indicates that the oxygen demand is greater than its delivery and that a heart attack may occur in future. If lifestyle changes and medication have not relieved the symptoms, or the narrowed coronary arteries are at imminent risk of a heart attack, coronary bypass surgery or angioplasty is performed.

blocks.title: Recovery and risk
blocks.text: Recovery from a heart attack is possible if the damaged portion of the heart is small enough that the other blood vessels in the heart can enlarge their capacity and resupply the damaged tissue. Heart disease and coronary artery disease are the leading causes of death in developed countries.

Coronary bypass surgery is one of the most common and effective procedures to compensate for the blockage of blood to the cardiac muscle. The surgeon takes a healthy blood vessel from the leg, arm, chest or abdomen of the patient and attaches its ends above and below the blocked coronary artery, so that blood is bypassed around the damaged or blocked area. Open or beating-heart surgery is done while the heart is still beating. Bypass surgery does not cure the underlying disease process, atherosclerosis or coronary artery disease: lifestyle changes, especially stopping smoking, are crucial to reduce the chance of future blockages and heart attacks even after successful surgery, and patients also need to reduce certain types of fat in the diet, increase physical activity, and control high blood pressure, diabetes and the other risk factors for heart disease.

blocks.text: Angioplasty is a procedure that opens a blocked or narrowed artery. A small wire, the catheter, is passed under X-ray guidance through the narrowed coronary artery, and a small sausage-shaped balloon is advanced over the wire into the narrowed section and inflated to dilate it; once the artery is dilated, a small amount of dye is injected to confirm the successful dilatation. Stenting may also be done during angioplasty: a stent is an expandable stainless steel mesh tube mounted on a balloon catheter. When the stent and balloon are positioned within the narrowed artery the balloon is inflated, expanding the stent and the artery; the balloon is removed and the stent remains in place, supporting the artery walls and keeping the artery open and dilated.

blocks.text: A chronic (long-lasting) elevation of blood pressure is hypertension, which occurs when blood pressure consistently remains above 140/90. Any abnormality in the nervous or hormonal mechanisms of blood pressure regulation may cause it; other causes include stress, obesity, high salt intake and smoking, and there may also be hereditary reasons. Whenever blood pressure is chronically elevated there is an increased chance of the rupture of blood vessels; when this occurs in the brain it is a brain haemorrhage, which damages the delicate structure of the brain. Hypertension also weakens the cardiac muscle: if it is prolonged the heart is unable to pump effectively and the blood flow cannot be maintained to meet the needs of the tissues, so blood may be retained in the heart and lungs, in congestive heart failure. Hypertension can also damage the nephrons of the kidneys, which leads to further retention of salts and water in the blood and therefore further hypertension.

blocks.title: Chest pain and heart failure
blocks.text: Chest pain, including angina, does not occur during congestive heart failure.
